nameStory: This moss gets its 'feather' name from the way its delicate branches spread out like tiny green feathers across tree bark and rocks. The 'clustered' part refers to how it grows in dense, bunched patches rather than spreading out in loose mats like many other mosses.
description: Clustered Feather-moss is a small but striking moss that forms dense, feathery patches on tree bark, rocks, and logs. It grows in intricate, branching patterns that look like miniature fern fronds or bird feathers pressed flat against surfaces. Individual patches are typically just a few inches across, with the moss itself rarely growing more than an inch tall. When moist, it displays a vibrant green color that can seem almost jewel-like against dark bark.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms dense, feathery patches with regularly branched stems that lie flat against surfaces like tiny green feathers

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Tiny oval leaves overlap like shingles along the stems, creating a rope-like texture that feels smooth when you gently brush it with your finger

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright emerald green when wet, fading to yellowish or brownish-green when dry, with a subtle glossy sheen

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Almost exclusively grows on tree bark, especially smooth-barked trees like maples and beeches, occasionally on rocks

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels velvety-smooth to the touch when moist, becoming slightly crispy and brittle when completely dry

idTips.label: Sporophytes
idTips.description: Produces curved, reddish-brown capsules on thin stalks in late winter to early spring, though these are rarely seen

habitat: This moss thrives on the bark of deciduous trees throughout New England's forests, particularly favoring smooth-barked species like sugar maple, American beech, and yellow birch. It's most common in humid, shaded woodlands from sea level to mid-elevations, often growing alongside other bark-dwelling mosses and lichens. You'll rarely find it on very rough bark or in exposed, sunny locations.

seasonality.spring: Becomes most vibrant and noticeable as humidity increases, with sporophytes occasionally visible on thin reddish stalks. This is when the moss is most actively growing.
seasonality.summer: Remains green and visible in shaded areas but may appear duller and more compressed during dry spells. Look for it on the shadiest, most humid sides of trees.
seasonality.fall: Often shows renewed growth and color as autumn rains arrive, becoming lush and bright green again after summer dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Stays visible year-round but appears more brownish-green and compressed, still maintaining its distinctive feathery branching pattern even under snow.

funFact: Despite being tiny, this moss can live for decades on the same tree, slowly expanding its feathery empire one microscopic leaf at a time — a single patch the size of your palm might represent 20 years of patient growth!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other feathery bark mosses, but Clustered Feather-moss grows in distinctly dense, tightly-packed clusters rather than loose, spreading mats. Memory trick: 'Clustered' means crowded together — if the feathery moss looks like it's all bunched up trying to fit in a small space, you've likely found this species.
compareHints: Unlike its relative Steerecleus Moss, Clustered Feather-moss forms much denser, more compact patches and has a stronger preference for smooth tree bark over rocks and logs. The branching pattern is also more regular and feather-like, while Steerecleus tends to have more irregular, sprawling growth. [Note: Limited reference material available for this uncommon species — field verification recommended.]

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its relative Clustered Feather-moss, Steerecleus Moss has more distinctly serrated leaf edges and grows in looser, less organized mats.
